beats.caption: Analog chips are everywhere the board meets the real world
beats.text: Analog chips handle continuous quantities: voltage, current, temperature, sound, radio. On this GPU board the VRM controller, the current-sense amplifiers in each phase, the regulators for small rails and the fan drivers are all analog or mixed-signal. The bench lays one complete chain out in a row.

beats.caption: A sensor gives a tiny, noisy signal
beats.text: A temperature sensor on the hot inductor puts out a few millivolts that drift with heat, buried in electrical noise from the switching around it. Nothing digital can use it yet.

beats.caption: Amplify, then filter
beats.text: An operational amplifier multiplies the signal a hundredfold with precise, stable gain. A filter of resistors and capacitors then strips the high-frequency noise, leaving a clean, slow wave. Precision here is the hard part: microvolt offsets and low drift over years and temperature.

beats.caption: Convert, decide, and drive something physical
beats.text: An ADC turns the clean wave into numbers, a microcontroller decides the fan must speed up, and a driver chip turns its command back into real power: pulses that spin the fan's motor. Analog sits at both ends of every such loop.

beats.caption: Made on old fabs, sold for decades
beats.text: Analog parts rarely need leading-edge transistors; many are made on 200 mm and older 300 mm lines that are long paid off. Thousands of products sell to thousands of customers for 10-20 years, so margins are high and the business follows industrial and auto cycles. Makers: TI (TXN), Analog Devices (ADI), Microchip (MCHP), NXP (NXPI), onsemi (ON).
